sources: Scientific American, Fact or Fiction?: A Cockroach Can Live without Its Head (C. Choi, 2007), quoting entomologist Christopher Tipping (Delaware Valley College) and physiologist Joseph Kunkel (UMass Amherst): decapitated American cockroaches, necks sealed, lasted several weeks in a jar; open circulatory system with low pressure, necks often seal by clotting; they breathe through spiracles in body segments without needing the brain; can survive weeks on one meal; eventually die of mold, bacteria or virus; https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/fact-or-fiction-cockroach-can-live-without-head/

UC Berkeley News, Cockroach inspires robot that squeezes through cracks (2016, Jayaram and Full, PNAS): cockroaches compress to about a quarter of their standing height, about two stacked pennies; withstand forces of 900 times their body weight without injury; https://news.berkeley.edu/2016/02/08/cockroach-inspires-robot-that-squeezes-through-cracks/

University of Kentucky Entomology, Cockroach Control Manual (ENTFACT-614): German cockroach most common indoors; most active at night, hide in cracks near food, warmth and moisture; eat nearly all human food plus soap, toothpaste, glue, hair; up to 40 young hatch from one German cockroach egg case; one mated female can produce thousands of cockroaches in less than a year; droppings and shed skins cause allergies and can trigger asthma, especially in children; can spread microbes that cause food poisoning; https://entomology.mgcafe.uky.edu/ef614

beats.say: A cockroach can live for weeks without its head.
The cockroach. And it's in your kitchen, after dark.
It doesn't need a head to breathe. Air goes in through little holes along its body.
And its blood runs at such low pressure that the neck often just clots shut.
In one lab, headless roaches lasted weeks in a jar.
It just never gets to eat again.
At night it comes out of the cracks, looking for food.
And it eats almost anything. Your crumbs. Your soap. Glue. Toothpaste. Even hair.
It can flatten itself to a quarter of its height.
That's a gap as thin as two stacked pennies.
Berkeley scientists found it can take forces 900 times its body weight, and walk away.
One egg case can hatch up to forty babies.
One female can start thousands of roaches in less than a year.
And here's the part nobody thinks about. Their droppings and shed skins float in the air.
For some kids, that can trigger asthma.
They also track germs from the trash onto your food.
So, you see one on the counter. Would you stomp it, or run?
Just don't count on the head to finish it off.
